newsitem.title: CHINA: China growth seen at 9.8 pct, reserves at $140 bln.
newsitem.headline: China growth seen at 9.8 pct, reserves at $140 bln.

text.p: China's economy will grow 9.8 percent this year, and strong capital inflows will push its foreign exchange reserves to $140 to 150 billion by the year-end, the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council said.

The council, a Singapore-based policy forum, said in its Pacific Economic Outlook that the growth in gross domestic product will be recorded amid a continued policy of moderately tight monetary control.
The council's economic growth forecast compares with a recent forecast of 10 percent by a senior Chinese economist and an actual 9.7 percent recorded in 1996.
The economic outlook, seen in Beijing, also put 1998 growth at a slightly slower nine percent.

It predicted inflation this year would be 6.3 percent. China has forecast retail price inflation of 6.0 percent this year, compared with 6.1 percent in 1996, but price rises so far have been well below these levels.
Some Chinese economists say retail price inflation could be three to four percent this year.

The council said that despite the increasing cost of doing business in China, the momentum of capital inflow will continue and China will remain by far the world's top destination for foreign direct investment.
It said foreign direct investment should be about equal to last year's roughly $40 billion.
Steady inflows of investment capital coupled with a favourable trade picture gave China foreign currency reserves of $105 billion at the end of last year.
The total rose to $115 billion by the end of April, according to the official media.
China will face difficulties in increasing its exports and this will have a negative impact on imports, the council said.
It said total foreign trade will rise at a rate of six to seven percent though no trade deficit is expected.
China had a trade surplus of $10.29 billion in the January-April period this year and a surplus of $12.24 billion for all of last year.
The council said, however, that China faced structural problems in its shift to a market economy from central planning.
It said economic power was still linked to political power, adding that future stability was not assured.

Reform of the inefficient and debt-saddled state-owned enterprise system was said to be a matter of urgency. Despite 18 years of economic reform, the state enterprise system had not changed fundamentally.
